title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given an m × n matrix, return all of its elements in spiral order: across the top row left to right, down the last column, back across the bottom row right to left, up the first column, then repeat on the rectangle that remains.
realWorld: Serialising a 2-D region into a 1-D stream in a fixed order — image tiles written to a file, sensor cells read in a coverage sweep, or a robot vacuum planning a boundary-first path over a room grid.

examples.explanation: Top row 1,2,3 → right column 6,9 → bottom row 8,7 → left column 4 → the single remaining cell 5.
After the outer ring, only the middle row [6,7] is left, and it is walked left to right.
A single row. The bottom-row pass must be skipped, or 2 and 1 would be emitted a second time — this is the case the guards exist for.

constraints: The matrix is not necessarily square

bruteForce.idea: Simulate a walker with a visited grid. Step in the current direction; when the next cell is off the edge or already visited, turn right.

if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols || visited[nr][nc]) {
dir = (dir + 1) % 4;              // blocked — turn right and re-probe
bruteForce.whySlow: The time is already optimal — every cell must be emitted, so nothing can beat O(m·n). The cost is the second grid: `boolean[][] visited` is exactly as large as the input and exists only to remember where the walker has been. The turn logic is also error-prone, since a blocked step must be detected, the direction rotated, and the step recomputed, and getting that sequence slightly wrong produces a walk that looks almost right.

patternIdentification: The traversal order is prescribed, not discovered — this is a simulation, not a search. Whenever the shape of the walk is known in advance, the positions already visited are implied by the walk itself, so the visited structure is redundant. A spiral is four straight passes over a rectangle that shrinks by one on each side per round, which four integers describe completely.

optimized.idea: Hold the inclusive bounds of the unvisited rectangle in `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`. Walk each of the four edges, moving that boundary inwards afterwards. The two `if` guards before the bottom and left passes are essential: once the rectangle has narrowed to a single row or column, the top and right passes have already consumed it, and walking it again emits every element twice.
code: if (matrix == null || matrix.length == 0 || matrix[0].length == 0) return out;
int top = 0, bottom = matrix.length - 1;        // matrix.length  = rows
int left = 0, right = matrix[0].length - 1;     // matrix[0].length = columns
for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(matrix[top][c]);        // → top row
for (int r = top; r <= bottom; r++) out.add(matrix[r][right]);      // ↓ right column
for (int c = right; c >= left; c--) out.add(matrix[bottom][c]);  // ← bottom row
for (int r = bottom; r >= top; r--) out.add(matrix[r][left]);    // ↑ left column
int top = 0, bottom = rows - 1, left = 0, right = cols - 1;
for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(matrix[top][c]);
for (int r = top; r <= bottom; r++) out.add(matrix[r][right]);
// guard 1: without this, a single remaining row is walked twice
if (top <= bottom) for (int c = right; c >= left; c--) out.add(matrix[bottom][c]);
// guard 2: without this, a single remaining column is walked twice
if (left <= right) for (int r = bottom; r >= top; r--) out.add(matrix[r][left]);

commonMistakes: Omitting the `if (top <= bottom)` and `if (left <= right)` guards. A square test matrix hides the bug completely; `[[1,2,3]]` returns 1,2,3,2,1 and `[[1],[2],[3]]` returns 1,2,3,2.
Using `matrix.length` for the column count. On a square input it compiles, runs and quietly produces a transposed spiral; on a 2×5 input it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Shrinking a boundary before the pass that uses it, rather than after — the first row then never gets emitted.
Writing the bottom and left passes with ascending loops. They run in reverse: `c` from `right` down to `left`, and `r` from `bottom` down to `top`.
Not guarding the empty input. `matrix[0].length` throws when `matrix.length == 0`.
Looping `while (out.size() < rows * cols)` and forgetting to break inside the passes — the guards are still needed, and this form makes the off-by-one harder to see.
